# Dimension 3: Open-Source and Commercial Models

Source details: [../citations.md](../citations.md)

---

## 1. The a16z "Never Another Red Hat" Thesis

The thesis holds that pure open-source companies that rely solely on support and services (the Red Hat model) are difficult to scale and defend [59]. The preferred alternative is **open-core**: release a community edition freely while reserving enterprise features (SSO, RBAC, compliance, audit logging, advanced security) behind commercial licensing [59] [69].

Enterprise features "serve as critical differentiators that justify premium pricing" [69]. Growth-stage opportunities center on "platform plays where network effects, data governance, and platform security create a durable moat" [69].

Collective market capitalization of open-source-based companies (GitLab, Confluent, Databricks, MongoDB, Elastic, Snyk, HashiCorp, MuleSoft): approximately **$100 billion** [60].

## 2. Architecture Determines Commercial Attack Surface

How a product is architected directly affects how easily competitors and cloud providers can replicate or commoditize it. This thesis links Dimensions 1 and 3.

### Monolithic Open-Core: GitLab Model

GitLab ships as a **single application** with feature gating via license keys [60]. The entire codebase is in one repository. Features are differentiated by tier (Free, Premium, Ultimate) using internal feature flags, not architectural separation [60].

**Defensibility characteristics:**
- Easy to adopt and self-host as a single artifact
- Difficult for cloud providers to strip enterprise features — they are woven into the monolith
- High adoption due to ease of use, but also high free-rider potential since the entire codebase is visible

### Distributed Open-Core: Confluent Model

Confluent separates the open-source Apache Kafka from proprietary components (Confluent Control Center, Schema Registry management, RBAC) that are architecturally distinct services [61].

**Defensibility characteristics:**
- Cloud providers can offer vanilla Kafka without Confluent's proprietary management plane
- But Confluent's SaaS grew at **180% vs 46% for on-prem** [61], showing managed service is the real moat
- Developer adoption of open-source Kafka leads to enterprise Confluent Cloud purchases: "developers recommend the enterprise versions to their bosses" [68]

### Plugin Architecture: Terraform/HashiCorp

HashiCorp's Terraform uses a plugin (provider) architecture where the core is open-source but the ecosystem of providers and enterprise features creates lock-in. HashiCorp's subsequent **BSL license change** demonstrated the tension: when cloud providers commoditize the open-source core, the company restricts the license [62] [63].

## 3. License Changes as Defensive Moves

Multiple database companies have changed licenses in response to cloud provider commoditization:

| Company | Change | Rationale | Consequence |
|---------|--------|-----------|-------------|
| Redis | OSS to source-available (then added AGPLv3) | "The majority of Redis' commercial sales were channeled through the largest cloud service providers, who commoditize Redis' investments" [62] | 75% of surveyed users testing/considering Valkey fork [64]; CEO admitted licensing "damaged the company's relationship with its community" [62] |
| MongoDB | AGPL to SSPL | Prevent cloud providers from offering MongoDB-as-a-service without contributing back | AWS created DocumentDB as alternative |
| Elastic | Apache 2.0 to SSPL + Elastic License | AWS OpenSearch fork | Community split |
| HashiCorp | MPL to BSL | Prevent competitive hosted offerings | OpenTofu fork created |
| InfluxDB | Removed clustering from OSS edition | Reserve scaling capabilities for enterprise | Self-hosters limited to single-node |

**Pattern**: license restrictions protect revenue but risk community fracture and fork creation. The Redis case shows this can be partially reversed (AGPLv3 re-addition) but at the cost of trust [62] [64].

## 4. Baldwin & Clark: Modularity and Free-Riding

The academic literature on modularity theory (Baldwin & Clark) establishes that **modular architectures enable selective free-riding on components** [70]. When a system is decomposed into independent modules with clean interfaces:

- Competitors can substitute individual modules while relying on the rest of the ecosystem
- Cloud providers can host the open-source core without the proprietary management/enterprise modules
- Users can adopt the free tier and build their own replacements for paid components

This creates a fundamental tension: **modularity improves the software** (easier to maintain, test, evolve) **but also improves the ability of others to extract value without paying** [70].

## 5. The Self-Hosting Economics

### The Cost Calculus

- Engineering time is the "highest hidden cost of self-hosting infrastructure" [71]
- Average developer at ~$75/hour spending 3-5 hours/month per server = $225-$375 in labor costs [71]
- Managed hosting premium of $50-$100/month is often more cost-effective [71]
- Decision heuristic: "If this service is critical to your business, this is the core of your business! If the service is not critical... you should use a hosted version" [72]

### Architecture Affects Self-Hosting Difficulty

| Architecture | Self-Hosting Difficulty | Why |
|-------------|------------------------|-----|
| Monolith | Lower | Single artifact, single deployment, single database |
| Modular monolith | Lower | Same as monolith with internal module structure |
| Microservices | Higher | Multiple services, orchestration, service discovery, distributed tracing |

The implication for commercial strategy: **easy-to-run = high adoption but high free-rider risk**. Complex-to-run = lower adoption but higher conversion to paid managed service [65].

### The Sentry Model

David Cramer (Sentry co-founder): Sentry commercializes via affordable hosted cloud service. "The fact that you can self-host Sentry creates defensibility from upstarts competing with them" [67]. The open-source codebase is visible, but running it at scale with reliability is hard enough that most choose the paid hosted option.

## 6. Complexity-as-Lock-In Strategy

Developers may "intentionally or strategically make open source software difficult to build, deploy, or fully use without additional tools, services, or expertise" [65]. "Unlike dual-licensing or proprietary add-ons, complexity-as-lock-in leverages practical friction rather than legal restrictions to generate revenue" [65].

This is controversial: "Critics argue that this strategy can limit adoption and contradict the spirit of open source, while proponents note that it balances community access with sustainable revenue models" [65].

The InfluxDB approach of removing clustering from the OSS edition is the clearest example — the software works for development and small-scale use, but production-grade deployment requires the commercial offering.

## 7. The Central Tension

| Goal | Favors | Risk |
|------|--------|------|
| Maximum adoption | Easy to self-host (monolith, simple deployment) | High free-rider rate; cloud providers offer hosted versions |
| Revenue protection | Hard to self-host (complex architecture, enterprise features gated) | Lower adoption; community frustration; fork risk |
| Ecosystem moat | Plugin architecture, integrations, marketplace | Slower to build; requires critical mass |
| License protection | Restrictive licenses (SSPL, BSL) | Community backlash; fork creation (Valkey, OpenTofu) |

The most successful COSS companies navigate this tension by offering a **managed service that is genuinely better** than self-hosting, rather than making self-hosting artificially hard [67] [66].
